What is the difference between a process and a thread?
column2: A process is a running program with its own address space, open files and a process control block. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of the same process share code, heap and files but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between because no new address space is needed and the TLB isn't flushed. The cost is safety: a bug or race in one thread can corrupt the whole process, so shared data needs synchronisation.

column1: What happens during a context switch?
column2: The kernel saves the running task's CPU state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) into its PCB or thread control block, picks the next task with the scheduler, restores that task's saved state and, if it belongs to another process, switches the page tables, which also invalidates TLB entries. Context switches are pure overhead, which is why too small a round-robin time quantum hurts throughput.

column1: What are the four conditions for deadlock, and how do you prevent it?
column2: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait; all four must hold. Prevention breaks one of them. In practice the easiest is circular wait: acquire locks in one fixed global order. Others: request all resources at once (breaks hold and wait), or allow preemption. Avoidance (Banker's algorithm) only grants a request if the system stays in a safe state. Detection builds a wait-for graph and recovers by killing or rolling back a process.

column1: Mutex vs semaphore?
column2: A mutex is a lock with an owner: one thread locks it and the same thread must unlock it, giving mutual exclusion for a critical section. A semaphore is a counter with wait (decrement, block at zero) and signal (increment). A counting semaphore lets up to N threads use N identical resources, like a pool of 5 database connections. A binary semaphore looks like a mutex but has no owner, so it's also used for signalling between threads, for example producer to consumer.

column1: What is virtual memory and why is it used?
column2: Each process sees a private, contiguous address space. The MMU translates virtual pages to physical frames through page tables, with the TLB caching recent translations. Benefits: isolation between processes, running programs larger than RAM by keeping only the working set in memory, simpler loading and linking, and sharing (shared libraries, copy-on-write after fork). The cost is translation overhead and page faults.

column1: What is a page fault and what is thrashing?
column2: A page fault occurs when a process touches a page that isn't in RAM. The OS traps, finds the page on disk, picks a victim frame with a replacement policy such as LRU, loads the page, updates the page table and restarts the instruction. Thrashing is when the combined working sets don't fit in memory, so the system spends most of its time paging instead of executing. Fixes: reduce the degree of multiprogramming or add memory.

column1: Compare FCFS, SJF and round robin scheduling.
column2: FCFS runs jobs in arrival order; simple but short jobs wait behind long ones (convoy effect). SJF picks the shortest burst and gives the minimum average waiting time, but needs burst estimates and can starve long jobs. Round robin gives each process a time quantum in turn: good response time for interactive systems; the quantum must be large relative to the context-switch cost. Real systems use multilevel feedback queues or Linux's CFS.

column1: What is a race condition, and what is a critical section?
column2: A race condition is when the result depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data, for example two threads doing count++ (load, add, store) and losing an update. The critical section is the code that touches the shared data. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting, implemented with locks, semaphores or atomic operations.

column1: What are zombie and orphan processes?
column2: A zombie has finished but its parent hasn't called wait() to read its exit status, so its process-table entry remains. An orphan's parent died first; it's re-parented to init or systemd, which reaps it. Many zombies can exhaust process IDs, so parents must wait() or handle SIGCHLD.

column1: What do fork() and exec() do?
column2: fork() creates a child that is a copy of the parent; modern kernels share pages copy-on-write until either side writes. It returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. exec() replaces the current process image with a new program, keeping the PID and open file descriptors. A shell runs a command with fork, then exec in the child, while the parent waits.

column1: Internal vs external fragmentation?
column2: Internal fragmentation is wasted space inside an allocated block, for example the unused part of the last page. External fragmentation is enough total free memory split into pieces too small to use, typical of variable-size allocation and segmentation. Paging removes external fragmentation at the cost of some internal fragmentation.

column1: Explain normalisation up to 3NF with an example.
column2: Take Student(roll, name, dept, dept_head). 1NF: every value is atomic, no repeating groups. 2NF: no non-key column depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: no non-key column depends on another non-key column. dept_head depends on dept, not on roll, so it's a transitive dependency; split into Student(roll, name, dept) and Dept(dept, dept_head). This removes update anomalies: changing a head now touches one row.

column1: What are the ACID properties?
column2: Atomicity: a transaction happens fully or not at all, using undo logs. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if run one after another, to the chosen isolation level. Durability: once committed, data survives crashes, using write-ahead logging. Example: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another; atomicity stops money disappearing if the system crashes in between.

column1: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads? Explain the anomalies.
column2: A dirty read is reading another transaction's uncommitted data; a non-repeatable read is the same row returning different values within one transaction; a phantom read is a repeated range query returning new rows. Read Committed prevents dirty reads, Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads, and Serializable prevents phantoms. Higher isolation costs concurrency. PostgreSQL and MySQL implement these with MVCC snapshots.

column1: How does an index speed up a query, and why B+ trees?
column2: Without an index the database scans every row. A B+ tree index keeps keys sorted in wide, shallow nodes sized to disk pages, so finding a key among millions takes about 3 to 4 page reads, and range queries walk the linked leaf level. Hash indexes are faster for exact matches but can't do ranges. Indexes speed reads but slow inserts and updates and use space.

column1: Clustered vs non-clustered index?
column2: A clustered index determines the physical order of the rows; there's one per table, usually the primary key. A non-clustered (secondary) index is a separate structure storing the key plus a pointer or the primary key, so lookups may need a second step. A covering index includes all columns the query needs and avoids that step.

column1: Primary key vs unique key vs foreign key?
column2: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and can't be null; one per table. A unique key also enforces uniqueness but allows null (one or many nulls depending on the database) and a table can have several. A foreign key references another table's key and enforces referential integrity, for example orders.user_id must exist in users.id.

column1: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?
column2: DELETE removes chosen rows with WHERE, is logged row by row, fires triggers and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly by deallocating pages, usually can't use WHERE and resets identity counters. DROP removes the table itself along with its structure, indexes and constraints.

column1: Write SQL for the second-highest salary per department.
column2: Use a window function: SELECT dept_id, name, salary FROM (SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r FROM employee e) t WHERE r = 2. DENSE_RANK handles ties so two people sharing the top salary don't push the second-highest to rank 3. Without window functions, use a correlated subquery counting distinct higher salaries.

column1: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
column2: WHERE filters rows before grouping and can't use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates, for example SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5. The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY.

column1: SQL vs NoSQL: when would you choose each?
column2: SQL databases give a fixed schema, joins and strong ACID transactions: good for payments, orders, anything relational. NoSQL stores (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) give flexible schemas and easier horizontal scaling, often with eventual consistency: good for huge write volumes, caching, feeds and logs. Many systems use both, for example PostgreSQL for orders and Redis for sessions.

column1: How do you prevent SQL injection?
column2: Never build queries by concatenating user input. Use parameterised queries or prepared statements, where the query structure and the data are sent separately, so input can't change the query. Add least-privilege database accounts and input validation as extra layers.

column1: What happens when you type google.com and press Enter?
column2: The browser checks its caches, then resolves the name through DNS: OS cache, then a recursive resolver that asks the root, the .com TLD server and Google's authoritative server, returning an IP. The browser opens a TCP connection (three-way handshake) or QUIC, then a TLS handshake that checks Google's certificate and agrees keys. It sends an HTTP GET; the request may pass a CDN and load balancer to an application server. The response HTML is parsed, CSS, JS and images are fetched, and the page is laid out and painted.

column1: Explain the TCP three-way handshake. Why not two?
column2: Client sends SYN with sequence number x; server replies SYN-ACK with its own sequence y and ack x+1; client sends ACK y+1. Three messages are needed so both sides know the other received their initial sequence number. With two, the server couldn't tell whether the client got its SYN, and an old duplicate SYN could open a ghost connection.

column1: TCP vs UDP, and when would you use UDP?
column2: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: ordered delivery, acknowledgements, retransmission, flow and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantees and very little overhead. Use UDP when latency matters more than perfect delivery: video calls, online games, live streaming, DNS lookups. QUIC (HTTP/3) adds reliability on top of UDP to avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking.

column1: Flow control vs congestion control?
column2: Flow control protects the receiver: the receiver advertises a window of how much it can buffer, and the sender never exceeds it. Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window that grows with slow start and additive increase, and shrinks sharply on packet loss (multiplicative decrease).

column1: Explain the OSI model and where common devices sit.
column2: Physical (bits on the wire), data link (frames, MAC addresses, switches), network (IP packets, routing, routers), transport (TCP/UDP, ports), session, presentation and application (HTTP, DNS). TCP/IP merges them into link, internet, transport and application. Each layer adds its own header: data, then segment, packet and frame.

column1: How does HTTPS work?
column2: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. In TLS 1.3 the client and server exchange ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key shares to derive a shared secret; the server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority, which the client verifies. After the handshake, traffic is encrypted and integrity-protected with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM. Asymmetric crypto is used only to authenticate and agree keys because it's slow.

column1: What is DNS and which record types matter?
column2: DNS maps names to addresses through a hierarchy of servers with caching controlled by TTLs. A maps to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME aliases one name to another, MX gives mail servers, NS names authoritative servers, TXT holds text such as SPF records. It mostly uses UDP port 53, falling back to TCP for large responses.

column1: What is subnetting? How many hosts in a /26?
column2: Subnetting splits a network by borrowing host bits for the network part. A /26 leaves 32 − 26 = 6 host bits: 2⁶ = 64 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, so 62 usable hosts. Subnetting limits broadcast domains and lets you apply security rules per subnet, like public and private subnets in an AWS VPC.

column1: What is ARP, and what is ARP spoofing?
column2: ARP finds the MAC address for an IP on the local network: a host broadcasts 'who has 192.168.1.1?' and the owner replies with its MAC. ARP has no authentication, so an attacker can send forged replies and become the man in the middle. Defences include dynamic ARP inspection on switches and encrypting traffic with TLS.

column1: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3?
column2: HTTP/1.1 sends requests one after another per connection (browsers open several connections). HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, but a lost TCP packet still blocks all streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, so streams are independent and connection setup is faster.

column1: Explain the four pillars of OOP with examples.
column2: Encapsulation: keep data private and expose methods, like a BankAccount whose balance changes only through deposit and withdraw. Abstraction: show what an object does, not how, like an abstract Shape with area(). Inheritance: a Circle is a Shape and reuses its interface. Polymorphism: calling area() on a Shape reference runs Circle's or Square's version at run time through virtual functions; overloading and templates give compile-time polymorphism.

column1: Overloading vs overriding?
column2: Overloading is the same function name with different parameter lists in the same scope, resolved at compile time. Overriding is a derived class redefining a base class's virtual function with the same signature, resolved at run time through the vtable. In C++, mark overrides with the override keyword so the compiler catches signature mistakes.

column1: How does a virtual function call work in C++?
column2: Each class with virtual functions has a vtable, an array of pointers to its versions of those functions. Each object holds a hidden vptr to its class's vtable, set by the constructor. A virtual call loads the vptr, indexes the vtable and jumps: one extra indirection that usually prevents inlining.

column1: Why should a base class destructor be virtual?
column2: If you delete a derived object through a base pointer and the destructor isn't virtual, only the base destructor runs; the derived part's resources leak and the behaviour is undefined. Any class meant to be used polymorphically should have a virtual destructor.

column1: Abstract class vs interface?
column2: In C++ an abstract class has at least one pure virtual function (= 0) and can't be instantiated; it can still have data and implemented methods. An interface is the special case with only pure virtual functions and no data. Java and C# have a separate interface keyword; C++ uses abstract classes for both.

column1: What is RAII?
column2: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime. The constructor acquires (memory, file, lock) and the destructor releases, so cleanup happens automatically even when an exception is thrown. unique_ptr, lock_guard and ifstream are RAII types; it's why modern C++ rarely needs raw new and delete.

column1: unique_ptr vs shared_ptr?
column2: unique_ptr has one owner, can be moved but not copied, and has no overhead over a raw pointer. shared_ptr allows many owners through a reference count and frees the object when the count reaches zero; it costs an atomic counter and can leak through cycles, which weak_ptr breaks. Default to unique_ptr.

column1: Explain SOLID briefly.
column2: Single responsibility: one reason to change. Open/closed: extend behaviour without editing existing code, through interfaces. Liskov substitution: a subclass must work anywhere its base does (a Square that breaks Rectangle's setters violates it). Interface segregation: small focused interfaces. Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions and inject concrete implementations.

column1: Shallow copy vs deep copy?
column2: A shallow copy copies member values, so two objects end up pointing at the same heap memory, leading to double frees. A deep copy allocates new memory and copies the pointed-to data. If a class owns a raw resource, follow the rule of three/five (destructor, copy and move operations), or use RAII members like vector so the defaults are correct.

column1: What is a static member, and what is const correctness?
column2: A static data member belongs to the class, not to any object, so all instances share it; a static member function has no this pointer. Const correctness means marking anything that shouldn't change as const: const references for parameters you only read, and const member functions that promise not to modify the object.

column1: Operating Systems: Process?
column2: A program in execution with its own address space, PCB, registers and open files.

column1: Operating Systems: Thread?
column2: A unit of execution inside a process; threads share code, heap and files but have their own stack and registers.

column1: Operating Systems: Context switch?
column2: Saving one process's CPU state in its PCB and loading another's; pure overhead.

column1: Operating Systems: Scheduling?
column2: FCFS, SJF/SRTF (optimal average wait, can starve), Round Robin (time quantum), Priority (aging prevents starvation).

column1: Operating Systems: Deadlock?
column2: Needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Handle by prevention, avoidance (Banker's), detection or ignoring.

column1: Operating Systems: Semaphore vs mutex?
column2: Mutex: a lock with an owner. Semaphore: a counter with wait/signal; binary or counting.

column1: Operating Systems: Paging?
column2: Fixed-size pages map to frames via a page table; no external fragmentation; TLB caches translations.

column1: Operating Systems: Virtual memory?
column2: Demand paging lets programs exceed RAM; a page fault loads a missing page; thrashing = too few frames.

column1: Operating Systems: Page replacement?
column2: FIFO (Belady's anomaly), LRU, Optimal (theoretical best), Clock (LRU approximation).

column1: Operating Systems: System call?
column2: A trap from user mode into kernel mode, e.g. fork, exec, read, write, mmap.

column1: DBMS: Keys?
column2: Super key ⊇ candidate key (minimal) ⊇ primary key (chosen, unique, not null). Foreign key references another table's key.

column1: DBMS: Normalisation?
column2: 1NF atomic values; 2NF no partial dependency; 3NF no transitive dependency; BCNF every determinant is a candidate key.

column1: DBMS: ACID?
column2: Atomicity (all or nothing, undo log), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrency control), Durability (redo / write-ahead log).

column1: DBMS: Isolation levels?
column2: Read uncommitted < read committed (no dirty reads) < repeatable read (no non-repeatable reads) < serializable (no phantoms).

column1: DBMS: Concurrency control?
column2: Two-phase locking gives serializability; strict 2PL also avoids cascading aborts; MVCC gives readers snapshots.

column1: DBMS: Indexes?
column2: B+ trees for range and equality lookups; hash for equality only; clustered = table order (one per table).

column1: DBMS: Joins?
column2: Inner, left, right, full outer, cross, self; executed as nested loop, hash join or merge join.

column1: DBMS: Transactions?
column2: BEGIN … COMMIT / ROLLBACK; savepoints; deadlocks found with a wait-for graph.

column1: DBMS: SQL vs NoSQL?
column2: Relational with schemas and joins vs key-value, document, column-family or graph stores that scale out easily.

column1: DBMS: CAP?
column2: Under a network partition a distributed store chooses consistency or availability.

column1: Computer Networks: OSI / TCP-IP?
column2: Application, (presentation, session), transport, network, data link, physical. TCP/IP merges the top three.

column1: Computer Networks: TCP?
column2: Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow control (receiver window) and congestion control (slow start, AIMD).

column1: Computer Networks: UDP?
column2: Connectionless, no ordering or retransmission, low overhead: DNS, video, games, QUIC underneath.

column1: Computer Networks: Handshake?
column2: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK to open; FIN / ACK in each direction to close; TIME_WAIT afterwards.

column1: Computer Networks: IP addressing?
column2: IPv4 32 bits, IPv6 128 bits; CIDR /n; private ranges 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16; NAT shares one public IP.

column1: Computer Networks: Routing?
column2: Routers forward by longest-prefix match; RIP (distance vector), OSPF (link state), BGP between networks.

column1: Computer Networks: ARP, DHCP, DNS?
column2: ARP: IP → MAC on the LAN. DHCP: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. DNS: name → IP, mostly UDP 53, cached by TTL.

column1: Computer Networks: HTTP?
column2: Stateless request/response; methods GET, POST, PUT (idempotent), PATCH, DELETE; status classes 1xx–5xx.

column1: Computer Networks: HTTPS / TLS?
column2: TLS handshake agrees keys and authenticates the server with a CA-signed certificate; data then uses symmetric encryption.

column1: Computer Networks: Devices?
column2: Hub (L1), switch (L2, MAC table), router (L3), load balancer (L4/L7).

column1: OOP and design: Encapsulation?
column2: Keep data private and expose behaviour through methods; protects invariants.

column1: OOP and design: Abstraction?
column2: Show what an object does, hide how: interfaces and abstract classes.

column1: OOP and design: Inheritance?
column2: 'Is-a' reuse; prefer composition ('has-a') when behaviour varies.

column1: OOP and design: Polymorphism?
column2: Compile-time: overloading, templates. Run-time: virtual functions via the vtable.

column1: OOP and design: Virtual destructor?
column2: Needed when deleting a derived object through a base pointer.

column1: OOP and design: Rule of 3 / 5 / 0?
column2: Destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment (+ move constructor, move assignment); or own nothing raw and need none.

column1: OOP and design: SOLID?
column2: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion.

column1: OOP and design: Patterns?
column2: Singleton, Factory, Builder (creational); Adapter, Decorator (structural); Strategy, Observer, State (behavioural).

column1: OOP and design: Object slicing?
column2: Copying a derived object into a base object by value loses the derived part.

column1: OOP and design: Smart pointers?
column2: unique_ptr (sole owner), shared_ptr (ref-counted), weak_ptr (breaks cycles); RAII frees resources.

column1: SQL: Order of execution?
column2: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

column1: SQL: WHERE vs HAVING?
column2: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups and can use aggregates.

column1: SQL: Joins?
column2: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps all left rows (NULLs on the right); anti-join: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL.

column1: SQL: NULL?
column2: Comparisons with NULL are unknown; use IS NULL; COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(*) does not; NOT IN breaks with NULLs.

column1: SQL: Subqueries and CTEs?
column2: Correlated subqueries run per row; WITH names an intermediate result; WITH RECURSIVE walks hierarchies.

column1: SQL: Window functions?
column2: ROW_NUMBER, RANK (gaps), DENSE_RANK (no gaps), LAG/LEAD, SUM() OVER (ORDER BY …) running totals.

column1: SQL: Set operations?
column2: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them; INTERSECT, EXCEPT.

column1: SQL: Indexes?
column2: Index columns in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY; check with EXPLAIN; composite index order matters (leftmost prefix).

column1: SQL: DDL / DML / DCL / TCL?
column2: CREATE, ALTER, DROP / SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE / GRANT, REVOKE / COMMIT, ROLLBACK.

column1: SQL: Classic patterns?
column2: Nth highest (DENSE_RANK or LIMIT OFFSET), top N per group, duplicates (GROUP BY HAVING COUNT > 1), consecutive days (date − row number).

column1: Which scheduling algorithm can starve long processes when short ones keep arriving?
column2: Shortest Job First. Short jobs always go first, so a long job can wait forever; aging fixes it.

column1: Which is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
column2: Preemption. The condition is no preemption; allowing preemption breaks deadlock.

column1: The Banker's algorithm is used for deadlock:
column2: Avoidance. It grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state.

column1: Thrashing happens when:
column2: Processes spend more time paging than executing. Too few frames per process causes constant page faults.

column1: Belady's anomaly (more frames, more faults) can occur with:
column2: FIFO. LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms and never show it.

column1: Reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with 3 frames under FIFO gives how many page faults?
column2: 9. With 4 frames it gives 10: the textbook Belady example.

column1: Same string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with 3 frames under LRU gives how many page faults?
column2: 10. Simulate: only the references 1, 2 after 5 hit.

column1: During a context switch the OS saves a process's registers in its:
column2: Process Control Block. The PCB holds registers, state, PC and scheduling information.

column1: Threads of the same process share:
column2: Heap and code. Each thread has its own stack, registers and PC.

column1: A semaphore initialised to 1 and used for mutual exclusion is a:
column2: Binary semaphore. Values 0 and 1 only; acts like a lock.

column1: A spinlock is the better choice when:
column2: The lock is held very briefly on a multiprocessor. Busy-waiting is cheaper than sleeping only for very short waits.

column1: The TLB is a cache of:
column2: Page-table entries. It speeds up virtual-to-physical address translation.

column1: 32-bit virtual addresses with 4 KB pages need how many entries in a single-level page table?
column2: 2^20. 32 − 12 offset bits leaves 20 bits of page number.

column1: Internal fragmentation occurs in:
column2: Paging. The last page of a process is partly unused.

column1: External fragmentation can be reduced by:
column2: Compaction. Compaction moves allocations together to merge free holes.

column1: A zombie process is one that:
column2: Has finished but its parent has not called wait(). Its exit status waits in the process table until reaped.

column1: Three fork() calls in a row (no conditions) leave how many processes in total?
column2: 8. Each fork doubles the count: 2^3.

column1: Round Robin with a very large time quantum behaves like:
column2: FCFS. No process is ever preempted.

column1: Bursts 24, 3, 3 arrive at time 0 in that order. Average waiting time under FCFS?
column2: 17. (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17. Under SJF it would be 3.

column1: The convoy effect is associated with:
column2: FCFS. Short jobs queue behind one long CPU-bound job.

column1: Peterson's solution solves the critical-section problem for how many processes?
column2: 2. It uses a turn variable and two flags.

column1: Bounded buffer of size N with semaphores empty, full, mutex. Initial values?
column2: empty = N, full = 0, mutex = 1. All slots start empty and the lock starts free.

column1: Which Unix system call creates a new process?
column2: fork(). exec() replaces the current image; it does not create a process.

column1: After a successful execvp(), the code that follows it in the program:
column2: Never runs. The process image is replaced; exec returns only on failure.

column1: A page fault occurs when a process accesses a page that is:
column2: Not in main memory. The OS then loads it from disk (demand paging).

column1: The dirty bit of a page is used to:
column2: Skip writing unmodified pages back to disk. Only modified pages must be written back on eviction.

column1: A system call normally enters the kernel through:
column2: A trap (software interrupt). The trap switches the CPU to kernel mode.

column1: SSTF disk scheduling can cause:
column2: Starvation of far requests. Requests near the head keep winning.

column1: Which is true of a mutex but not of a general semaphore?
column2: Only the thread that locked it may unlock it. A mutex has an owner; a semaphore does not.

column1: Virtual memory mainly allows:
column2: Running programs larger than physical memory. Only the needed pages are kept in RAM.

column1: Which normal form removes partial dependencies on a composite key?
column2: 2NF. 2NF: every non-key attribute depends on the whole key.

column1: Which normal form removes transitive dependencies?
column2: 3NF. 3NF: non-key attributes depend only on keys.

column1: A relation is in BCNF when:
column2: Every determinant is a candidate key. Stricter than 3NF.

column1: In ACID, the I stands for:
column2: Isolation. Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work.

column1: Which mechanism mainly provides durability?
column2: Write-ahead logging. The log is flushed before commit so changes survive a crash.

column1: The lowest isolation level that prevents dirty reads is:
column2: Read Committed. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads.

column1: In the SQL standard, phantom reads are prevented only at:
column2: Serializable. Repeatable Read still allows phantoms in the standard.

column1: Two-phase locking guarantees:
column2: Conflict serializability. 2PL can still deadlock; strict 2PL also avoids cascades.

column1: A primary key must be:
column2: Unique and not NULL. It identifies each row.

column1: A foreign key refers to:
column2: A primary or unique key in another (or the same) table. It enforces referential integrity.

column1: Which statement removes the table definition itself?
column2: DROP. DELETE and TRUNCATE remove rows only.

column1: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
column2: HAVING. WHERE filters rows before grouping.

column1: A CROSS JOIN of a 4-row table and a 5-row table returns how many rows?
column2: 20. Every pair: 4 × 5.

column1: A has 5 rows, B has 3, and no rows match. A LEFT JOIN B returns how many rows?
column2: 5. All left rows are kept, with NULLs for B.

column1: A column holds 1, NULL, 3, NULL. COUNT(column) returns:
column2: 2. COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) would return 4.

column1: B+ trees suit database indexes mainly because:
column2: High fan-out keeps them shallow and linked leaves make range scans fast. Fewer disk reads per lookup.

column1: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
column2: One. It defines the physical order of rows.

column1: A view is:
column2: A stored query that behaves like a virtual table. Materialised views are the exception that store results.

column1: A weak entity is one that:
column2: Cannot be identified without its owner entity. It has a partial key plus the owner's key.

column1: A minimal super key is called a:
column2: Candidate key. Remove any attribute and it stops being unique.

column1: Which relational-algebra operator chooses columns?
column2: Projection (π). Selection chooses rows.

column1: A DBMS detects deadlock with a:
column2: Wait-for graph. A cycle in the graph means deadlock.

column1: Which protocol avoids cascading rollbacks?
column2: Strict 2PL. Write locks are held until commit, so nobody reads uncommitted data.

column1: UNION differs from UNION ALL in that UNION:
column2: Removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL is faster because it skips duplicate removal.

column1: In SQL, the expression NULL = NULL evaluates to:
column2: UNKNOWN (NULL). Use IS NULL to test for NULL.

column1: Which query returns the second-highest salary from table e?
column2: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM e WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM e). The largest value below the maximum.

column1: According to CAP, during a network partition a distributed store must choose between:
column2: Consistency and availability. Partitions cannot be ruled out, so C or A gives way.

column1: Sharding means:
column2: Splitting rows of a table across several servers. Horizontal partitioning across machines.

column1: Denormalisation is done to:
column2: Speed up reads at the cost of redundancy. Fewer joins at query time.

column1: Which window function ranks ties without leaving gaps?
column2: DENSE_RANK(). RANK gives 1, 1, 3; DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2.

column1: Routing between networks happens at which OSI layer?
column2: Network. Layer 3: IP addresses and routers.

column1: TCP belongs to which layer?
column2: Transport. Layer 4, end to end.

column1: How many segments does the TCP connection setup take?
column2: 3. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

column1: Which transport protocol is connectionless?
column2: UDP. UDP sends datagrams with no handshake.

column1: Ordinary DNS queries mostly use:
column2: UDP port 53. TCP 53 is used for large answers and zone transfers.

column1: Which protocol gives hosts an IP address automatically?
column2: DHCP. Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

column1: ARP maps:
column2: IP addresses to MAC addresses. Used on the local link.

column1: How many usable host addresses are in a /26 subnet?
column2: 62. 2^6 − 2 (network and broadcast).

column1: The subnet mask for /20 is:
Which address is private (RFC 1918)?
Broadcast address of 192.168.10.0/24?
column2: 192.168.10.255. All host bits set to 1.

column1: Network address of 10.1.5.77/22?
column2: 10.1.4.0. /22 blocks start at multiples of 4 in the third octet.

column1: Default port for HTTPS?
column2: 443. HTTP uses 80.

column1: ping uses which protocol?
column2: ICMP. Echo request and echo reply.

column1: TCP flow control uses:
column2: The receiver's advertised window. The sender never exceeds what the receiver can buffer.

column1: In TCP slow start the congestion window grows:
column2: Exponentially per round trip. It doubles every RTT until the threshold.

column1: Which device works at the data link layer?
column2: Switch. It forwards by MAC address.

column1: A MAC address is how many bits long?
column2: 48. Six bytes, written in hex.

column1: An IPv6 address is how many bits long?
Which protocol guarantees in-order delivery?
column2: TCP. Sequence numbers and retransmission.

column1: Go-Back-N with n-bit sequence numbers allows a maximum sender window of:
column2: 2^n − 1. One number must stay free to tell new frames from old.

column1: Selective Repeat with n-bit sequence numbers allows a maximum window of:
column2: 2^(n−1). Sender and receiver windows must not overlap.

column1: NAT mainly:
column2: Maps private addresses to a public address. Many hosts share one public IP.

column1: In HTTPS the server proves its identity with:
column2: A certificate signed by a trusted CA. The browser checks the certificate chain.

column1: Which HTTP method is idempotent?
column2: PUT. Repeating PUT leaves the same state.

column1: HTTP 403 means:
column2: The server understood the request but refuses to allow it. 401 is for missing or bad authentication.

column1: Before opening a TCP connection to a website, the browser usually must:
column2: Resolve the host name with DNS. It needs the server's IP address.

column1: Transmission time of a 1000-byte packet on a 1 Mbps link?
column2: 8 ms. 8000 bits / 10^6 bits per second.

column1: Wi-Fi uses which access method?
column2: CSMA/CA. Wireless stations cannot detect collisions while sending.

column1: The largest TCP port number is:
column2: 65535. Ports are 16-bit fields.

column1: Encapsulation means:
column2: Bundling data with the methods that use it and hiding internal state. Access specifiers enforce it.

column1: Runtime polymorphism in C++ is achieved with:
column2: Virtual functions. Calls resolve through the vtable.

column1: Compile-time polymorphism in C++ includes:
column2: Function overloading and templates. Resolved by the compiler.

column1: An abstract class in C++ is a class with:
column2: At least one pure virtual function. Declared as virtual f() = 0.

column1: Can you create an object of an abstract class?
column2: No. You can have pointers or references to it.

column1: Why make a base-class destructor virtual?
column2: So deleting through a base pointer runs the derived destructor. Otherwise behaviour is undefined.

column1: C++ solves the diamond problem with:
column2: Virtual inheritance. One shared base subobject.

column1: Default access of members in a C++ class is:
column2: private. In a struct it is public.

column1: With class D : B { }; B is inherited as:
column2: private. struct would default to public.

column1: Which cannot be virtual in C++?
column2: A constructor. The object does not have a vptr yet.

column1: Why must a copy constructor take its parameter by reference?
column2: Passing by value would call the copy constructor again, recursing forever. Compilers reject by-value copy constructors.

column1: The rule of three covers:
column2: Destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment. If you need one, you usually need all three.

column1: A shallow copy of an object that owns a raw pointer risks:
column2: A double free. Both objects delete the same memory.

column1: A friend function:
column2: Can access private members but is not a member. Friendship is granted, not inherited.

column1: A static data member is:
column2: Shared by all objects of the class. Defined once.

column1: Inside a static member function, this is:
column2: Not available. It is not tied to any object.

column1: Overriding requires that the derived function:
column2: Has the same signature as a virtual base function. Use override so the compiler checks.

column1: 'Subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is' is which SOLID principle?
column2: Liskov substitution. The L in SOLID.

column1: 'Open for extension, closed for modification' is the:
column2: Open/closed principle. Add new behaviour without editing tested code.

column1: Dependency inversion says high-level modules should depend on:
column2: Abstractions. Both sides depend on interfaces.

column1: Interface segregation says:
column2: Prefer several small interfaces to one large one. Clients should not depend on methods they do not use.

column1: A 'has-a' relationship is modelled by:
column2: Composition. Inheritance models 'is-a'.

column1: Which operator cannot be overloaded in C++?
column2: ::. Also . .* ?: and sizeof.

column1: The Singleton pattern ensures:
column2: A class has one instance with a global access point. Often criticised for hidden global state.

column1: The Factory pattern:
column2: Creates objects without the caller naming the concrete class. Callers depend on an interface.

column1: Which pattern notifies many objects when one object's state changes?
column2: Observer. Publish and subscribe.

column1: In a typical implementation, the vptr is stored:
column2: In each object of a class with virtual functions. Each object points to its class's vtable.

column1: Object slicing happens when:
column2: A derived object is copied into a base object by value. The derived part is cut off.

column1: The explicit keyword on a constructor:
column2: Prevents implicit conversions through it. Stops surprises like f(42) building an object.

column1: Correct syntax for a pure virtual function:
column2: virtual void f() = 0;. The = 0 marks it pure.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int a = 10, b = 3; cout << a / b << " " << a % b; }
column2: 3 1. Integer division truncates; 10 % 3 = 1.

column1: What does this print? int main() { cout << -7 / 2 << " " << -7 % 2; }
column2: -3 -1. Since C++11 division truncates toward zero and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int x = 5; int &r = x; r++; cout << x; }
column2: 6. r is another name for x.

column1: What does this print? int main() { char c = 'A' + 2; cout << c; }
column2: C. 'A' + 2 is 67, stored in a char, printed as a character.

column1: What does this print? int main() { unsigned int u = 0; u--; cout << (u > 0); }
column2: 1. Unsigned 0 − 1 wraps to the maximum value, which is > 0.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int a[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; cout << *(a + 2) << a[4]; }
What does this print? int main() { string s = "abc"; s += 'd'; cout << s.size() << s.back(); }
column2: 4d. Appending a char adds one to the size.

column1: What does this print? struct B { virtual void f() { cout << "B"; } virtual ~B() {} }; struct D : B { void f() override { cout << "D"; } }; int main() { B* p = new D; p->f(); delete p; }
column2: D. f is virtual, so the call uses the object's dynamic type.

column1: What does this print? struct B { void f() { cout << "B"; } }; struct D : B { void f() { cout << "D"; } }; int main() { D d; B* p = &d; p->f(); }
column2: B. Without virtual, the static type B picks the function.

column1: What does this print? struct A { A() { cout << "a"; } ~A() { cout << "~a"; } }; struct B : A { B() { cout << "b"; } ~B() { cout << "~b"; } }; int main() { B x; }
column2: ab~b~a. Base is built first and destroyed last.

column1: What does this print? struct B { virtual string n() { return "B"; } virtual ~B() {} }; struct D : B { string n() override { return "D"; } }; void show(B b) { cout << b.n(); } int main() { D d; show(d); }
column2: B. Passing by value slices D into a B.

column1: What does this print? int f() { static int c = 0; return ++c; } int main() { cout << f() << f() << f(); }
column2: 123. Since C++17 the operands of << are evaluated left to right; the static keeps its value.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int i = 0; for (; i < 5; i++); cout << i; }
column2: 5. The loop body is the empty statement after the semicolon.

column1: What does this print? int main() { cout << (7 & 3) << (7 | 8) << (5 ^ 1); }
What does this print? int main() { cout << (1 << 10); }
column2: 1024. 1 shifted left 10 times is 2^10.

column1: What does this print? int main() { vector<int> v{1, 2, 3}; v.push_back(4); v.erase(v.begin() + 1); for (int x : v) cout << x; }
column2: 134. erase(begin() + 1) removes the 2.

column1: What does this print? int main() { map<string, int> m; m["b"] = 2; m["a"] = 1; m["c"]; for (auto& [k, v] : m) cout << k << v; }
column2: a1b2c0. map is sorted by key; m["c"] inserts a value-initialised 0.

column1: What does this print? int main() { set<int> s{3, 1, 3, 2}; cout << s.size() << *s.begin(); }
column2: 31. set keeps unique sorted values {1, 2, 3}.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int a = 5; int* p = &a; *p += 2; cout << a; }
column2: 7. p points to a, so *p += 2 changes a.

column1: What does this print? int main() { cout << 5 / 2.0; }
column2: 2.5. One operand is double, so the division is floating point.

column1: What does this print? int main() { cout << (int)3.99 << (int)-3.99; }
column2: 3-3. Casting to int truncates toward zero.

column1: What does this print? int main() { bool b = (0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3); cout << b; }
column2: 0. 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point.

column1: What does this print? int main() { string s = "hello"; reverse(s.begin(), s.end()); cout << s.substr(1, 3); }
column2: lle. Reversed string is "olleh"; substr(1, 3) takes 3 chars from index 1.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int x = 10; auto f = [x]() mutable { return ++x; }; f(); cout << f() << x; }
column2: 1210. A mutable lambda changes its own copy of x; the outer x stays 10.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int x = 10; auto g = [&x] { x++; }; g(); g(); cout << x; }
column2: 12. Captured by reference, so each call changes x.

column1: What does this print? void f(int) { cout << "int"; } void f(double) { cout << "double"; } int main() { f('a'); }
column2: int. char to int is a promotion, which beats conversion to double.

column1: What does this print? int main() { priority_queue<int> pq; pq.push(3); pq.push(1); pq.push(4); cout << pq.top(); pq.pop(); cout << pq.top(); }
column2: 43. priority_queue is a max-heap by default.

column1: What does this print? int main() { int i = 0; if (i++ || i++) cout << i; }
column2: 2. The first i++ yields 0 (false), the second yields 1 (true); i is now 2.

column1: What does this print? struct A { A() { cout << "c"; } A(const A&) { cout << "k"; } A& operator=(const A&) { return *this; } }; int main() { A a; A b = a; A c; c = b; }
column2: ckc. A b = a copies (k); c = b is assignment, not construction.

column1: What does this print? int main() { cout << sizeof(char) << " " << sizeof("ab"); }
column2: 1 3. sizeof(char) is 1 by definition; the string "ab" has 3 bytes including '\0'.
